question: What is the medical term for a fit?
explanation: A fit is medically referred to as a seizure, which involves abnormal electrical activity in the brain. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T11#GNS222_U4_T11_h1)

question: When is a patient officially diagnosed with epilepsy?

options.A: After a single unprovoked seizure occurs
options.B: Whenever an abnormal EEG result is recorded
options.C: When a patient has a high fever with shaking
options.D: After two or more unprovoked seizures

explanation: Spot on! Doctors look for a pattern before diagnosing epilepsy—specifically, having two or more seizures that weren't triggered by an obvious cause like a high fever. You've got this! [learn more](GNS222_U4_T11#GNS222_U4_T11_h1)

question: What do we call the recovery period right after a seizure?

options.A: The permanent damage caused by fits
options.B: The exact moment a seizure begins
options.C: The recovery period right after a seizure
options.D: A test used to diagnose epilepsy

explanation: That phase right after a fit is called the postictal state. The brain is basically resting and resetting, which is why your patient might wake up feeling super tired or confused. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T11#GNS222_U4_T11_h2)

question: Why do patients often feel so exhausted and confused right after a major fit?

options.A: The seizure permanently destroyed parts of their memory
options.B: Their blood pressure dropped to dangerous levels
options.C: Their brain cells used up a lot of energy and need to recover
options.D: They received too much medication during the episode

explanation: Think of a seizure like a sudden electrical storm in the brain. It burns through so much energy that the brain needs some quiet time to recharge afterwards. Completely normal recovery! [learn more](GNS222_U4_T11#GNS222_U4_T11_h2)

question: Which type of seizure starts in only one specific area of the brain?
explanation: Focal seizures originate in a localized region of the brain, affecting only part of the body or awareness. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T11#GNS222_U4_T11_h3)

question: What is the main difference between focal and generalized seizures?

options.A: Whether they happen during sleep or waking hours
options.B: The type of medication used to stop them
options.C: Whether the patient has a fever
options.D: How much of the brain is involved at the start

explanation: It's all about location! A focal seizure starts in just one spot in the brain, while a generalized seizure involves both sides right from the beginning. Easy peasy! [learn more](GNS222_U4_T11#GNS222_U4_T11_h3)

question: What is the most common trigger for a breakthrough seizure in someone with epilepsy?
explanation: Consistency is key! Skipping meds lets the drug levels drop in the blood, making a seizure much more likely to happen. Remind your patients how important their schedule is. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T11#GNS222_U4_T11_h4)

question: A patient tells you they pulled a double shift, slept for only two hours, and now feel jittery. What should you suspect?

options.A: Severe sleep deprivation is lowering their seizure threshold
options.B: They are developing a severe bacterial infection
options.C: Their brain has permanently cured itself of epilepsy
options.D: They are experiencing side effects from low blood pressure

explanation: Rest is medicine! When patients don't get enough sleep, their brain's natural defense against seizures drops significantly. Always check on their sleeping habits. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T11#GNS222_U4_T11_h4)

question: Which diagnostic test specifically records the electrical activity of the brain?
explanation: An EEG uses electrodes placed on the scalp to detect and record abnormal electrical waves in the brain. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T11#GNS222_U4_T11_h5)

question: Why is talking to a witness so helpful when assessing a seizure?

options.A: Witnesses can prescribe the right medication immediately
options.B: The patient is usually unable to remember or describe the event themselves
options.C: Witnesses know the exact medical history of the patient
options.D: Doctors do not trust tests like the EEG

explanation: Since patients are often blanking out or unconscious during a fit, someone who watched it happen is your best source for piecing together what really went down! [learn more](GNS222_U4_T11#GNS222_U4_T11_h5)

question: What is the safest position for a patient right after a seizure stops?
explanation: Always roll them onto their side! This clever little nursing trick keeps saliva or vomit from blocking their airway and stops the tongue from falling back. Great job! [learn more](GNS222_U4_T11#GNS222_U4_T11_h6)

question: As a nurse, what should you NEVER do while a patient is actively having a fit?

options.A: Time how long the seizure lasts
options.B: Force objects between the patient's teeth
options.C: Loosen tight clothing around the neck
options.D: Clear hard objects away from the body

explanation: Never put anything in their mouth! You might accidentally chip their teeth, cut their gums, or block their airway even more. Just keep them safe and let the seizure run its course. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T11#GNS222_U4_T11_h6)

question: What is the main goal of taking anti-seizure medications?

options.A: To prevent future seizures by stabilizing brain activity
options.B: To permanently cure the underlying cause of epilepsy
options.C: To increase the speed of brain electrical signals
options.D: To immediately stop pain during a headache

explanation: These meds act like a steady anchor for the brain, calming down hyperactive nerve cells so seizures don't catch the patient off guard. You've got this concept down! [learn more](GNS222_U4_T11#GNS222_U4_T11_h7)

question: What can happen if a patient suddenly stops taking their anti-seizure medication?

options.A: It causes severe allergic skin reactions
options.B: It has no effect as long as the patient eats well
options.C: It can trigger dangerous rebound seizures or status epilepticus
options.D: It will immediately cause permanent memory loss

explanation: Abruptly quitting these drugs takes away the brain's chemical shield. It can easily lead to a scary rebound attack or even a medical emergency. Always educate patients to taper off only under doctor's orders! [learn more](GNS222_U4_T11#GNS222_U4_T11_h7)

question: How long does a seizure need to last to be called 'status epilepticus'?
explanation: Any seizure lasting past five minutes—or happening back-to-back without waking up—is an emergency called status epilepticus. Quick thinking is vital here! [learn more](GNS222_U4_T11#GNS222_U4_T11_h8)

question: A patient has been convulsing for eight minutes straight without waking up. What is your immediate nursing priority?

options.A: Wait quietly at the bedside until the patient stops moving on their own
options.B: Have the patient stand up and walk around to clear their head
options.C: Call for emergency medical help and prepare airway support and rescue medication
options.D: Ask the family members what the patient ate for breakfast

explanation: This is a true emergency! Prolonged seizures cut off vital oxygen to the brain, so you need to sound the alarm and grab rescue medication right away. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T11#GNS222_U4_T11_h8)

question: Why should a patient with uncontrolled epilepsy wear a medical alert bracelet?

options.A: To prove to the police that they can drive a car
options.B: To track how many hours of sleep they get each night
options.C: To store extra doses of anti-seizure medication
options.D: To ensure bystanders and emergency workers know what is wrong

explanation: If a patient can't speak for themselves after a fit, that little bracelet does the talking for them, making sure helpers know exactly what condition they have. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T11#GNS222_U4_T11_h9)

question: Which activity is generally not safe for someone with unmanaged seizures?

options.B: Reading books in a well-lit room

explanation: Safety first! If a seizure hits while swimming alone, the risk of drowning is extremely high. Advising against solo swimming is a crucial part of patient education. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T11#GNS222_U4_T11_h9)
